content.overview: Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 provides that when either the husband or the wife has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other, the aggrieved party may petition the district court for a decree of restitution of conjugal rights. The burden of proving reasonable excuse lies on the person who has withdrawn (Explanation). Non-compliance with a restitution decree for one year or more is a ground for divorce under s. 13(1A). Constitutional validity was upheld in Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha.

content.study:
Section 9 is the statutory remedy for restoration of consortium when one spouse has withdrawn from the society of the other without reasonable excuse.

Text: When either the husband or the wife has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other, the aggrieved party may apply, by petition to the district court, for restitution of conjugal rights and the court, on being satisfied of the truth of the statements made in such petition and that there is no legal ground why the application should not be granted, may decree restitution of conjugal rights accordingly.

Explanation: Where a question arises whether there has been reasonable excuse for withdrawal from the society, the burden of proving reasonable excuse shall be on the person who has withdrawn from the society.

The decree does not authorise physical detention or forced sexual relations. Its practical significance often lies in the fact that non-resumption of cohabitation for one year or more after the decree is a ground for divorce under s. 13(1A).

Constitutional challenges based on privacy and personal autonomy under Article 21 were raised in T. Sareetha v. T. Venkata Subbaiah (AP High Court). The Supreme Court in Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984) upheld the constitutional validity of s. 9, holding that the decree aims at restoration of marital companionship and does not compel sexual intercourse. Courts continue to apply the section with a rights-sensitive approach and will not grant restitution where cohabitation would be unjust or unsafe.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body:
Section 9 restates the classical remedy of restitution of conjugal rights in statutory form for Hindu marriages governed by the HMA.
Legislative objective: provide a civil mechanism to restore consortium when one spouse has withdrawn without reasonable excuse, while preserving the Court’s discretion to refuse the decree where there is a legal ground against it.
Doctrinal foundation: the remedy is based on the obligation of spouses to live together. Modern application is tempered by constitutional values of privacy, dignity and autonomy. The decree is not a licence for forced cohabitation or sexual relations; its primary practical effect is often the pathway to divorce under s. 13(1A) after non-compliance.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos & Statutory Deconstruction
sections.body:
Trigger: either spouse has withdrawn from the society of the other without reasonable excuse.
Remedy: petition by the aggrieved party to the district court for a decree of restitution of conjugal rights.
Court’s satisfaction: the Court must be satisfied of the truth of the statements in the petition and that there is no legal ground why the application should not be granted.
Explanation: the burden of proving reasonable excuse lies on the person who has withdrawn.
No sub-section (2) remains after the 1976 amendment; the earlier provision relating to execution was omitted.

sections.heading: Mandatory Proving Ingredients & Essential Elements
sections.body:
1. A valid marriage between the parties (governed by the HMA).
2. The respondent has withdrawn from the society of the petitioner.
3. The withdrawal was without reasonable excuse.
4. There is no legal ground why the application should not be granted (Court’s residual discretion).
Once withdrawal is established, the burden of proving reasonable excuse shifts to the respondent under the Explanation.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Burdens under BSA 2023 (ss. 104–106 & s. 63)
sections.body:
The petitioner must prove the fact of withdrawal from society on a preponderance of probabilities.
Once withdrawal is shown, the Explanation places the burden of proving reasonable excuse on the respondent. Reasonable excuse typically includes cruelty, conduct making cohabitation unsafe or improper, or other just cause.
Documentary and electronic evidence (messages, medical records, prior complaints) must satisfy ordinary admissibility rules, including BSA s. 63 for electronic records.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Competent Forum & Limitation Act Checkpoints
sections.body:
Competent court: District Court (or Family Court where established) having jurisdiction under the HMA / Family Courts Act.
Procedure: petition under s. 9 → evidence on withdrawal and reasonable excuse → decree if the Court is satisfied and no legal ground exists against the grant.
Consequence of non-compliance: if cohabitation is not resumed for one year or more after the decree, either party may seek divorce under s. 13(1A).
Appeal lies under the ordinary appellate provisions applicable to Family Court / District Court decrees.
No special limitation period is prescribed for a s. 9 petition beyond the general principles applicable to matrimonial petitions.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Restitution granted
examples.body: W leaves the matrimonial home without alleging cruelty, desertion by H, or any other excuse. H petitions under s. 9. The Court finds that W has withdrawn from H’s society without reasonable excuse and that there is no legal ground to refuse the decree. Restitution is granted.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Reasonable excuse established (petition fails)
examples.body: H petitions under s. 9. W proves continuous physical and mental cruelty by H. The Court holds that W’s withdrawal was with reasonable excuse. The petition is dismissed.

hypotheticals.question: Is the divorce petition maintainable?
hypotheticals.analysis:
1. A valid restitution decree under s. 9 exists.
2. Cohabitation has not been resumed for more than one year after the decree.
3. Section 13(1A) expressly provides that either party may present a petition for divorce on this ground.
4. The constitutional validity of s. 9 itself was upheld in Saroj Rani; the pathway to divorce under s. 13(1A) is a statutory consequence of non-compliance.

rows.right: Relieve the parties of the duty to cohabit while the marriage continues

rows.left: Withdrawal from society without reasonable excuse
rows.right: Any of the grounds available for divorce under s. 13

rows.left: Marriage continues; decree seeks restoration of living together
rows.right: Marriage continues but parties are no longer obliged to cohabit
Non-resumption of cohabitation for ≥ 1 year after decree → s. 13(1A)

misconceptions.trap: A restitution decree under s. 9 forces the respondent into physical cohabitation or sexual relations.
misconceptions.correction: The decree does not authorise physical detention or forced sexual relations. Its practical significance is often the statutory pathway to divorce under s. 13(1A) after non-compliance for one year or more.

misconceptions.trap: Section 9 is unconstitutional after the recognition of the right to privacy.
misconceptions.correction: The Supreme Court in Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha upheld the constitutional validity of s. 9. Courts apply the section with a rights-sensitive approach and refuse the decree where cohabitation would be unjust.

cases.name: Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha
cases.facts: Constitutional challenge to s. 9 of the HMA on the ground that a decree of restitution of conjugal rights violates the right to privacy and personal liberty under Article 21.
cases.issue: Whether s. 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is constitutionally valid.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Section 9 is constitutionally valid. The decree aims at restoration of marital companionship and does not compel sexual intercourse. The remedy is a means of encouraging reconciliation and is consistent with the scheme of the Act.
cases.holding: Constitutional validity of s. 9 upheld. The contrary view of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in T. Sareetha was overruled.
cases.relevance: Binding authority on the constitutionality of restitution of conjugal rights. Must be cited whenever the privacy / autonomy challenge is raised.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Explain restitution of conjugal rights under Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, including the burden of proof and the link to divorce under s. 13(1A).
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE
When may a spouse obtain a decree of restitution of conjugal rights, and what are the consequences of non-compliance?

II. GOVERNING RULE
Section 9 permits a decree where one spouse has withdrawn from the society of the other without reasonable excuse. The Explanation places the burden of proving reasonable excuse on the person who has withdrawn. Non-resumption of cohabitation for one year or more after the decree is a ground for divorce under s. 13(1A).

III. APPLICATION
Prove withdrawal → respondent must establish reasonable excuse → if no reasonable excuse and no legal ground against the decree, restitution may be granted. After one year of non-compliance, s. 13(1A) becomes available.

IV. CONCLUSION
Section 9 remains a valid civil remedy (Saroj Rani). Its practical significance often lies in the pathway to divorce after non-compliance.

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. STATEMENT OF FACTS
[Insert the facts of withdrawal and the acts constituting reasonable excuse (e.g. cruelty).]

II. STATUTORY SCHEME
Section 9 requires withdrawal without reasonable excuse. The Explanation places the burden of proving reasonable excuse on the person who has withdrawn.

III. APPLICATION
The respondent has discharged the burden by proving continuous cruelty / conduct making cohabitation unsafe. Withdrawal was therefore with reasonable excuse. The petition must fail.

IV. CONSTITUTIONAL CONTEXT
While Saroj Rani upheld the validity of s. 9, the Court retains discretion to refuse the decree where cohabitation would be unjust or unsafe. The present facts fall within that residual discretion.

V. PRAYER
[Dismissal of the petition under s. 9.]
